title: 当 AI 编写代码时，什么才算证据？
author: Elliot Gardiner
content:
Early in my career, a senior engineer showed me how to execute PHP from the command line instead of bringing up the entire web application to check a small change. That lesson changed how I approached debugging because I had learned a better method. Software teams preserve that kind of learning through conversations, code reviews, troubleshooting notes, and answers from people who have encountered a problem before. As coding agents perform more of the investigation themselves, I worry that we may get the patch while losing the lesson. An agent can encounter an error, search for an answer, try several remedies, discover a working route, and quietly move on. The developer receives changed files and a reassuring summary; the investigation often disappears.

That is a bigger problem than whether any single AI-generated pull request should pass its validation checks. Software engineering depends on a shared memory of failures: what went wrong, which diagnoses misled us, what finally worked, and which conditions made the difference. If agents solve these problems in private sessions that no one can search, we risk producing more code while keeping less useful knowledge for the next engineer.

The answer is faster; the learning is less visible

Stack Overflow's 2026 Developer Survey gives the tension some context. Among respondents asked how their usage of Stack Overflow had changed, 64.1% said they visit less often for simple questions and 28.9% reported asking fewer questions. Those are self-reported behavior changes rather than proof that AI agents caused a loss of institutional knowledge. The same survey found that 48% of respondents considering trust in AI said they trust the output when they can easily verify it. These results suggest a useful direction for developer tools: making answers and their supporting evidence easier to inspect and retrieve.

When I review code, I want to know what work led to the patch. The useful artifact is a compact explanation connected to real events. This is the structure of a good troubleshooting answer whether it lives on Stack Overflow, an internal Q&A site, or an engineering runbook.

A successful agent session can hide valuable failures

A deliberately staged case in the public grader-issue-lab repository makes the value of a failure record concrete. In pull request #10, organization lint and unit checks passed, as did the repository integration check, but the issue-specific authorization test failed. The code still raised `KeyError` for unknown order IDs, revealing whether an ID existed, while access to another customer's order was denied. The agent changed the implementation so both cases produced `AccessDenied`, reran the required checks, and obtained a passing gate. A final success report would have hidden the more instructive fact: the acceptance test caught a behavioral distinction the other checks did not exercise.

The store’s unit test deliberately expects KeyError for a missing order, while the integration test covers a customer reading their own order. The authorization acceptance test compares missing and foreign orders and requires the same exception and message. The repair catches KeyError in get_order_for_customer and raises AccessDenied("order not found"), leaving the storage contract and acceptance test unchanged. A reusable explanation could link those tests to the repair and tell the next contributor where to look: the function enforcing customer access.

The record preserves a precise security expectation that another contributor or agent may need: unknown orders and unauthorized orders must not be distinguishable to the caller. Recording the failed acceptance case, the reason it matters, and the subsequent verified change creates a small piece of reusable engineering knowledge.

The error message needs context

Consider an integration test that times out while connecting to a database. The string "connection timed out" could describe many unrelated root causes. A relevant knowledge match needs details about the driver, runtime, and diagnostic commands already attempted. Without that context, semantic search may find an extremely plausible answer to a different failure. The same issue arises with stack traces, build exceptions, permission errors, and flaky test assertions.

I've been exploring a product design that begins with failure facts captured from coding-agent sessions. The intended workflow groups recurring errors within the appropriate permissions, searches existing authorized knowledge sources, and presents likely matches with source citations and resolution status. When no suitable match exists, it drafts an answerable question for review. When an engineer eventually supplies a verified answer, the system could link that answer to future occurrences of the same kind of failure. This is a direction under development.

Search before you create another question

Automatically turning every error cluster into a new forum post would reproduce one of the oldest problems of technical Q&A: duplicates with slightly different wording and no maintained answers. A system should search first, recognizing the difference between an accepted answer that still applies, an obsolete workaround, and an unanswered thread. Similarity alone is not enough to declare a problem solved, particularly when the language or software version differs.

When a new question is appropriate, the agent's session can provide a better draft than a bare exception string. It can summarize expected and actual behavior, environment versions, a minimal reproduction, and what was already tried. It must remove secrets, sensitive source code, customer data, and anything the destination's readers are not authorized to see. It should also be candid about what is still unknown. A question with a reliable reproduction is an invitation for someone to help; a made-up diagnosis is another misleading search result.

An initially useful context is a company's private engineering knowledge repository, where administrators control the permitted sources, review modes, and posting identity. An unresolved failure should become a question; a confirmed reproducible defect might need an issue; and a validated fix might deserve a durable runbook. These are distinct forms of knowledge, and choosing among them matters more than the volume of content produced.

Development traces can become better explanations

Observability is useful because it distinguishes what an agent proposed from what it actually did. A trace can show the command that ran, the failure returned, the tool or environment used, and whether a later edit made the result stale. It can also expose repetitive attempts that consumed resources without making progress. For reusing knowledge, this means we can distinguish "someone suggested this command" from "this command produced this result under these conditions." That is the kind of evidence that allows the next developer to verify, challenge, and improve an explanation.

Let a verified answer improve the next agent

Today an agent may finish a task and leave its investigation behind; tomorrow another agent can encounter the same failure and begin from zero. If a reviewed explanation is associated with the error's context, the next agent can retrieve it at the point where it encounters the failure. A human correction can then become a reusable improvement in the development environment.

For this authorization case, a later agent adding a customer lookup could inspect the access contract and add a check covering both missing and foreign orders. It would need to exercise the new lookup after its final edit and connect the result to that revision.

I would evaluate this by what actually happens during later sessions. Did the next agent find the relevant answer, did the resolution apply to its environment, and was the repeated investigation shortened or avoided? Did an engineer confirm the suggestion helped, and did the same error recur after the supposed fix? Counting questions created is a poor success metric; so is counting answers synthesized by AI. Success means developers and agents solve recurring problems more effectively because the team retained what it learned.

Knowledge still needs an editor

Not every command that eventually succeeds tells us why it succeeded. An agent might change both an application and its test assertion and conclude that it fixed the original problem. If every recovered session automatically became a knowledge-base article, the system could fill with plausible but wrong conclusions. A person should be able to correct an overly broad explanation, add environment constraints, flag an obsolete workaround, and verify the actual root cause. The record should distinguish an idea that seems plausible, a workaround observed once, a fix reproduced independently, and an answer accepted by someone with domain expertise.

Human review keeps technical knowledge useful after the immediate incident has passed. Agents can prepare sanitized reproductions, group related errors, find likely duplicates, and direct the question to an appropriate expert. Humans contribute system context and the judgment needed to turn an observation into a credible explanation. That would extend Stack Overflow-style collaboration into the work agents already perform privately.

The answer should outlive the session

The lessons I learned as a junior engineer about testing stayed with me because another engineer showed me a better way to investigate a problem. Coding agents can perform remarkable amounts of investigation without a human watching every step. We now have an opportunity to preserve the parts of that investigation that would have been worth sharing with a colleague. A working patch is one output of a development session; a reusable explanation may be another, and sometimes it is the more valuable one.

aiSummary: 文章指出，当 AI 编程智能体自主解决问题时，我们必须保留解决方案背后的调查知识与证据，以维护团队共享的工程记忆，并支持未来验证。
oneSentenceSummary: 文章指出，当 AI 编程智能体自主解决问题时，我们必须保留解决方案背后的调查知识与证据，以维护团队共享的工程记忆，并支持未来验证。
summary: 文章探讨了 AI 编程智能体虽然能高效生成补丁，却也可能侵蚀软件团队赖以从失败中学习的共享知识。作者认为，调查过程——智能体如何发现并修复问题——与修复本身同样有价值。文章以 grader-issue-lab 仓库中的案例为例，说明智能体的一次成功修复最初掩盖了一个与安全密切相关的行为差异。作者提出，应建立能够记录失败事实、检索现有知识库，并在必要时生成结构清晰的问题的系统。文章强调，人类编辑者对于区分看似合理的想法与经过验证的修复至关重要；保留可复用的解释，既有利于人类开发者，也能帮助未来的智能体。文章还引用 Stack Overflow 2026 开发者调查的数据，为开发者行为的变化以及他们对 AI 输出的信任程度提供背景。

mainPoints.point: AI 编程智能体能够高效解决问题，但可能丢弃团队过去通过代码审查和故障排查记录所积累的宝贵调查知识。
mainPoints.explanation: 智能体遇到错误、查找解决方案，然后悄然继续工作时，调查过程便会消失，只留下补丁。这可能导致软件工程赖以发展的失败共享记忆流失。

mainPoints.point: 失败记录及其背景对于保存工程知识至关重要，未来的贡献者或智能体可能会用到这些知识。
mainPoints.explanation: 文章通过一个案例说明，智能体的修复最初掩盖了一个与安全密切相关的差异：订单不存在与订单未获授权并非一回事。记录未通过的验收案例、失败原因以及经过验证的改动，可以沉淀关于访问控制要求的可复用知识。

mainPoints.point: 系统应记录失败事实、检索现有知识库，并在找不到合适匹配项时生成结构清晰的问题。
mainPoints.explanation: 文章提出了一种工作流：归纳反复出现的错误，检索经授权且附有引用来源的信息，并拟定包含环境详情和已尝试解决方案的问题，同时移除敏感数据。

mainPoints.point: 人类编辑者对于区分看似合理的想法与经过验证的修复，并维护技术知识库的质量不可或缺。
mainPoints.explanation: 并非每条成功执行的命令都能说明成功的原因。人工审查可以修正过于宽泛的解释，补充环境限制，标记已过时的权宜方案，并核实真正的根本原因。

mainPoints.point: 保留可复用的解释有助于人类开发者和未来的智能体减少重复调查、提高效率。
mainPoints.explanation: 如果经过审查的解释与错误发生时的背景关联起来，后续智能体遇到同一故障时就能检索到它，从而避免重复调查并提高效率。

keyQuotes: 「可用的补丁是一次开发过程的成果之一；可复用的解释也可能是另一项成果，有时它更有价值。」
「软件工程依赖共享的失败记忆：出了什么问题、哪些诊断误导了我们、最终什么办法奏效，以及哪些条件造成了差异。」
「这份记录保留了一项精确的安全要求，其他贡献者或智能体可能会用到：对于调用方而言，不存在的订单与未获授权的订单必须不可区分。」
「人类审查能让技术知识在当前事件过去后仍然有用。」
「成功意味着开发者和智能体能够更有效地解决反复出现的问题，因为团队保留了从中学到的经验。」
